projectSummary: The most direct retrieved press-versus-fly activation contrast. It is a dumbbell fly, not a cable fly, and it is a tier-4 acute proxy: master plan section 2.2 forbids reading it as a hypertrophy comparison.

publication.statusSource: PubMed record comments-and-corrections fields plus the Crossref/Retraction Watch CSV export, fetched 2026-09-13

notes: Abstract-only, so normalisation reference, electrode placement and crosstalk handling could not be verified; the repository's own methods source says standard bipolar surface EMG mischaracterises this muscle.
The load is 6RM in each exercise, so the absolute external load differs between conditions by design.
Whole-muscle pectoralis sampling; no portion resolution.

Access level corrected on 2026-09-13 from abstract-only to full-text-open. The first pass stopped at the Europe PMC fullTextXML endpoint, which returns 404 for this record; ladder step 2 also names PubMed Central itself, and the article body is served there (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7675616/, 175892 bytes). The earlier level understated what was lawfully readable.

Amplitude was compared without normalisation to any reference contraction. Un-normalised RMS amplitude is comparable within a subject between two similar exercises, which is what the authors claim, but it cannot be read as a measure of how hard the muscle worked relative to its capacity, and it cannot be pooled with normalised studies. This is a material methodological limitation that the first pass recorded as unverifiable.

study.population: Seventeen resistance-trained men, age 22.9 (SD 1.8) years, height 1.80 (SD 0.06) m, body mass 80.0 (SD 8.3) kg, with 4.8 (SD 2.0) years of resistance-training experience.

title: A Comparison of Muscle Activation between Barbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Flyes in Resistance-Trained Males.
